distractors.0: Correct. `=` takes effect immediately, so `q2 = q1` reads the `q1` that was just assigned `d`, and `q3 = q2` reads that same value again. All three end the edge holding `d`. The synthesiser infers three flip-flops that are all fed from `d` — one stage of delay, in triplicate.
distractors.1: This is what `<=` would give, and it is why the bug is so easy to write: the *intent* is obvious from the code and the semantics do not match it. With non-blocking assignment all three right-hand sides are evaluated before any left-hand side is updated, so `q2` gets the old `q1` and the chain works.
distractors.2: No. An `always @(posedge clk)` block infers flip-flops regardless of which assignment operator is used — it is the clock edge in the sensitivity list that makes the logic sequential, not the operator. Blocking assignments in a clocked block are a *correctness* hazard, not a reason for registers to disappear. (Blocking assignment in a combinational `always @(*)` block is the correct choice, which is the other half of the rule.)
distractors.3: No, though there is something real behind it. With blocking assignments the *order of the statements* genuinely matters, and writing them in reverse — `q3 = q2; q2 = q1; q1 = d;` — does produce a working shift register. That is precisely why blocking assignment is dangerous: the code's behaviour depends on statement order in a way that hardware does not, so a reorder that looks harmless changes the circuit.

explanation:
## All three get `d` on the same edge

`=` is **blocking**: the assignment completes before the next statement runs, so later statements see the new value.

```
q1 = d;     ->  q1 is now d
q2 = q1;    ->  reads the NEW q1, so q2 is now d
q3 = q2;    ->  reads the NEW q2, so q3 is now d
```

One clock edge, and all three registers hold `d`. The design has one stage of delay implemented three times over. In simulation the waveform shows `q1`, `q2` and `q3` moving together, which looks like a routing problem and is not.

## The fix is one character per line

```verilog
always @(posedge clk) begin
    q1 <= d;
    q2 <= q1;
    q3 <= q2;
end
```

`<=` is **non-blocking**: every right-hand side is evaluated first, using the values as they were at the clock edge, and only then are the left-hand sides updated. So `q2` gets the *old* `q1`, and the chain works.

Crucially, the statements can now be in any order and the circuit is identical — which is exactly how hardware behaves. Three flip-flops do not care what order you listed them in.

## The rule, which has no useful exceptions

> **Clocked logic (`always @(posedge clk)`): use `<=`.**
> **Combinational logic (`always @(*)`): use `=`.**
> **Never mix the two for the same signal in the same block.**

Cliff Cummings' paper *Nonblocking Assignments in Verilog Synthesis, Coding Styles That Kill* is the canonical treatment, and the title is not hyperbole — mixing them is the most reliable way to produce a design that simulates differently from the hardware it synthesises to.

## Why the language is like this at all

Verilog is a *simulation* language that is also used for synthesis, and the two assignment operators exist because an event-driven simulator has to decide what happens when several things change at the same instant.

Real flip-flops all sample at the same moment and all update at the same moment. Non-blocking assignment models that: evaluate everything, then update everything. Blocking assignment models a sequence of steps, which is what you want when describing combinational logic as a computation but is not what a bank of flip-flops does.

The deeper lesson, and the one that transfers: **you are describing hardware, not writing a program.** An `always` block is not a function body executing top to bottom — it is a description of a circuit, and the statement order inside it should not matter. When it does matter, that is the signal you have written something that will not mean the same thing to the simulator and the synthesiser.

## How it gets caught

- The synthesis log reports the inferred registers; three flops all driven by `d` is visible there if you read it.
- Lint tools (Verilator with `-Wall`, or SpyGlass) flag blocking assignment in a clocked block directly. Verilator is free and will say so.
- In simulation, a shift register whose stages move together is the symptom. Looking at it on a waveform is faster than reasoning about it.
